source_text: «Omnes ergo animae penes inferos?» inquis. Velis ac nolis, et supplicia jam illic, et refrigeria. Habes pauperem et divitem. Et quia distuli nescio quid ad hanc partem, jam opportune in clausula reddam. Cur enim non putes animam, et puniri, et foveri in infernis interim sub expectatione utriusque judicii, in quadam usurpatione et candida ejus? «Quia salvum debet esse, inquis, judicio divino negotium suum, sine ulla praelibatione sententiae. Tum quia et carnis operienda est restitutio, ut consortis operarum atque mercedum.» Quid ergo fiet in tempore isto? dormiemus? Atenim animae nec in viventibus dormiunt: corporum enim est somnus, quorum et ipsa mors cum speculo suo somno. Aut nihil vis agi illic, quo universa humanitas trahitur, quo spes omnis sequestratur? Delibari putas judicium, an incipi? praecipitari, an praeministrari? Jam vero, quam iniquissimum etiam apud inferos, si et nocentibus adhuc illic bene est, et innocentibus nondum? Quid? ampliationem vis esse post mortem, confusa spe et incerta exspectatione ludentem, an vitae recensum jam et ordinationem judicii inhorrentem? Semper autem exspectat anima corpus, ut doleat, aut gaudeat? Nonne et de suo sufficit sibi ad utrumque titulum passionis? Quotiens, illaeso corpore, anima sola torquetur bile, ira, taedio, plerumque nec sibi noto! quotiens item corpore adflicto furtivum sibi anima gaudium exquirit, et a corporis importuna tunc societate secedit! Mentior, si non de ipsis cruciatibus corporis et gloriari et gaudere sola consuevit. Respice ad Mutii animam, cum dexteram suam ignibus solvit. Respice ad Zenonis, cum illam Dionysii tormenta praetereunt. Morsus ferarum ornamenta sunt juventutis, ut in Cyro ursi cicatrices. Adeo novit et apud inferos anima et dolere et gaudere sine carne; quia et in carne illaesa si velit dolet, et laesa si velit gaudet. Hoc si ex arbitrio suo in vita, quanto magis ex judicio Dei post mortem! Sed nec omnia opera cum carnis ministerio anima partitur; nam et solos cogitatus et nudas voluntates censura divina persequitur: Qui viderit ad concupiscendum, jam adulteravit in corde. Ergo propter hoc congruentissimum est animam, licet non exspectata carne, puniri, quod non sociata carne commisit. Sic et ob cogitatus pios et benevolos, in quibus carne non eguit, sine carne recreabitur. Quid nunc, si et in carnalibus prior est, quae concipit, quae disponit, quae mandat, quae impellit? Et, si quando invita, prior tamen tractat, quod per corpus actura est. Nunquam denique conscientia posterior erit facto. Ita huic quoque ordini competit, eam priorem pensare mercedes, cui priori debeantur. In summa, cum carcerem illum, quem Evangelium demonstrat, inferos intelligamus, et novissimum quadrantem modicum quodque delictum mora resurrectionis illic luendum interpretemur; nemo dubitabit animam aliquid pensare penes inferos, salva resurrectionis plenitudine per carnem quoque. Hoc etiam Paracletus frequentissime commendavit, si quis sermones ejus ex agnitione promissorum charismatum admiserit. Ad omnem, ut arbitror, humanam super anima opinionem, ex doctrina fidei congressi, justae dumtaxat ac necessariae curiositati satisfecimus. Enormi autem et otiosae tantum deerit discere, quantum libuerit inquirere.
thought_title: The Soul's Experience in the Afterlife
pass_a_gloss: Are all souls therefore among the dead, you ask. Willingly or unwillingly, there are already both punishments and refreshments there. You have the poor and the rich. And because I have delayed something to this part, I will now opportunely render it in the conclusion. For why should you not think that the soul is both punished and comforted in the underworld in the meantime under the expectation of both judgments, in a certain usurpation and candid judgment of it. Because, you say, the divine judgment ought to keep its business safe without any prelibation of the sentence. Then also because the restoration of the flesh must be worked out, so that it may be a partner of works and rewards. What therefore will happen in that time, shall we sleep. For souls do not sleep even in the living, for sleep is of bodies, of which even death is a mirror of sleep. Or do you think that nothing is done there, to which all humanity is drawn, to which all hope is entrusted. Do you think that judgment is being deliberated, or is it beginning, is it being hastened, or is it being served. Now indeed, how most unjust even in the underworld, if it is well with the guilty who are still there, and not yet with the innocent. What, do you want there to be an extension after death, with a confused hope and uncertain expectation playing, or a reckoning of life and an ordination of judgment already shuddering. But does the soul always expect the body, so that it may grieve or rejoice. Does it not suffice for itself to both titles of passion, even from its own. How often, with the body unharmed, the soul alone is tormented by bile, anger, disgust, often even without it being known to itself. How often, with the body afflicted, the soul seeks for itself a furtive joy, and withdraws from the importunate society of the body. I lie, if the soul is not accustomed to glory and rejoice alone even in the torments of the body. Look at the soul of Mucius, when he freed his right hand from the fires. Look at the soul of Zeno, when he passed by the torments of Dionysius. The bites of wild beasts are ornaments of youth, as the scars of the bear on Cyrus. So much does the soul know how to grieve and rejoice without flesh even in the underworld, because even in unharmed flesh it grieves if it wishes, and in harmed flesh it rejoices if it wishes. If this is from its own judgment in life, how much more from the judgment of God after death. But the soul does not share all its works with the ministry of the flesh, for divine censure also pursues solitary thoughts and naked wills. He who has looked at something to desire it, has already committed adultery in his heart. Therefore, it is most congruent that the soul, even if not expecting the flesh, is punished, because it has committed something not in partnership with the flesh. So also, because of pious and benevolent thoughts, in which the flesh did not cooperate, it will be comforted without the flesh. What now, if it is prior even in carnal things, which it conceives, which it arranges, which it commands, which it impels. And if sometimes it is unwilling, it is still prior in handling what it will do through the body. Finally, conscience will never be posterior to the deed. So it is also fitting for this order, that it weighs the rewards first, to which they are owed. In sum, when we understand that prison, which the Gospel shows, to be the underworld, and we interpret the last little quadrant, that every small fault is to be paid for there by the delay of the resurrection, no one will doubt that the soul pays something among the dead, with the fullness of the resurrection saved through the flesh also. The Paraclete also commended this most frequently, if someone has admitted his sermons from the recognition of the promised gifts. To every human opinion about the soul, having met from the doctrine of faith, we have satisfied just and necessary curiosity. But to enormous and idle curiosity, it will be lacking to learn as much as it pleased to investigate.

pass_b_english: So you're asking whether all souls go straight to the underworld? Willingly or not, punishments and refreshments are already happening there. You've got the poor and the rich. I've held something back for this section, so I'll deliver it now, right where it belongs. Why shouldn't you think the soul is both punished and comforted in the underworld while it waits for both judgments, operating under a kind of provisional, candid assessment? You say divine judgment must keep its case intact without any pre-tasting of the sentence. And then there's the resurrection of the flesh, which has to be worked out so the body can share in the works and the rewards. So what happens in the meantime? Do we sleep? Souls don't sleep, not even in the living. Sleep belongs to bodies, and death itself is just sleep's mirror. Or do you think nothing happens in the place where all humanity is dragged and every hope is held in escrow? You imagine judgment is being deliberated, or just beginning, rushed, or served up? Tell me, how monstrously unjust it would be even in the underworld if the guilty are still comfortable there while the innocent get nothing yet. What do you want? An extension after death, with confused hope and uncertain expectation toying with you? Or a reckoning of your life and a sentence already shuddering into place? Does the soul always wait for the body to feel grief or joy? Doesn't it have enough from itself for both kinds of suffering? How often, with the body unharmed, the soul alone is tortured by bile, rage, disgust, often without even knowing why? How often, with the body wrecked, the soul steals a private joy and slips away from the body's demanding company? I'd be lying if the soul weren't accustomed to boasting and rejoicing even in bodily torments—all on its own. Look at Mucius's soul when he thrust his right hand into the flames. Look at Zeno's soul when he walked past Dionysius's tortures. Wild beast bites are decorations of youth, like the bear scars on Cyrus. The soul knows perfectly well how to suffer and rejoice without flesh even in the underworld, because even in unharmed flesh it suffers if it chooses, and in harmed flesh it rejoices if it chooses. If it can do that by its own will in life, how much more by God's judgment after death? But the soul doesn't share all its works with the body's service. Divine scrutiny also pursues solitary thoughts and naked wills: anyone who has looked to lust has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5:28). So it's entirely fitting that the soul be punished even without the body, because it sinned without the body's partnership. Likewise, it will be comforted without the body for pious and benevolent thoughts in which the flesh had no share. What if the soul leads even in carnal matters, the one that conceives, arranges, commands, impels? Even when unwilling, it still handles first what it will do through the body. Conscience is never posterior to the deed. So the proper order requires that the one who is owed the rewards first should weigh them first. In short, once we understand that the prison the Gospel shows is the underworld, and that the final small quadrant where every minor fault is paid off by the resurrection's delay—no one will doubt the soul pays something among the dead, with the fullness of the resurrection preserved through the flesh as well. The Paraclete has urged this most frequently, if anyone has received his sermons through recognition of the promised gifts of the Spirit (John 14:26). For every human opinion about the soul, having met the doctrine of faith, we have satisfied just and necessary curiosity. But for enormous and idle curiosity, it will fall short of learning as much as it pleased to investigate.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex theological arguments regarding the soul's state between death and resurrection. Scripture citations (Matthew 5:28 and John 14:26) were correctly added to the English text to identify the allusions in the Latin. The title 'The Soul's Experience in the Afterlife' correctly names the thought of the chapter.
